subtitle: A request to document the drawing and visualization equipment available at each network site.

tldr.problem: The network community lacked centralized information about graphics capabilities available at different sites.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel requested that each site's technical liaison document their graphics facilities for inclusion in the Resources Notebook.
tldr.outcome: The request helped establish a resource inventory process for the developing network.

today: RFC 268 documents an administrative process from the very early ARPA network in November 1971. It represents the pre-digital documentation practices of the emerging network research community.

sections.title: The Request
sections.content:
Following a network graphics meeting at Stanford in November 1971, Jon Postel of UCLA-NMC sent this request to all network sites. He asked that each site's technical liaison provide a description of their graphics facilities for inclusion in the Resources Notebook, a centralized information repository that was being developed for the ARPA network.

The request was straightforward and administrative in nature. It aimed to create a catalog of graphics resources available across the nascent network, helping researchers discover and access visualization and drawing capabilities at remote sites.
sections.eli5: Jon Postel asked everyone to list what computers they had for drawing pictures.

sections.title: The Resources Notebook
sections.content:
The Resources Notebook was an early attempt to document the capabilities and services available at different ARPA network sites. It served as a reference for researchers who wanted to know what facilities and systems existed elsewhere on the network, helping them collaborate and share resources.

The Notebook was maintained through normal editorial procedures. Postel emphasized that this graphics facilities documentation would work alongside existing update mechanisms, not replace them, ensuring consistency with the broader resource inventory effort.
sections.eli5: The Resources Notebook was a big list of what equipment and tools each site had to offer everyone else on the network.

sections.title: Early Network Coordination
sections.content:
This RFC exemplifies the organizational work that underpinned the early ARPA network. Before automated discovery systems or standardized catalogs, humans maintained these records by collecting information from each site and compiling it centrally.

The effort shows how the network was not just technical infrastructure, but required community coordination. Graphics facilities ranged widely across the early network's universities and research institutions, making such documentation important for those seeking visualization and display capabilities.
sections.eli5: Each research center had different drawing tools, so keeping a list helped scientists find what they needed.
